items.title: Focus Question: A lab lists three solid samples: sample A (energy gap 0 eV, bands overlap), sample B (gap 1.4 eV), and sample C (gap 8.5 eV). How do conductors, insulators, and semiconductors differ, and which sample is which?

body.html: Band theory. Conductivity depends on the energy gap between the valence band and the conduction band.

A conductor has overlapping or partly filled bands, so electrons move freely. A semiconductor has a small gap (about 1 eV), so some electrons are excited across it. An insulator has a large gap (about 5 eV or more), so almost no electrons reach the conduction band. Sample A has no gap, sample B has a gap near 1 eV, and sample C has a gap well above 5 eV.

answer.html: A is a conductor, B is a semiconductor, and C is an insulator.

check.html: The ordering of gap sizes (0, 1.4, 8.5 eV) matches the ordering of conductivity from highest to lowest.

items.title: Figure 1 prompt: A graph of energy gap versus atomic separation passes through (0.14 nm, 6.0 eV) and (0.26 nm, 1.0 eV), and the gap falls steadily between these points. Estimate the energy gap at an atomic separation of 0.18 nm

body.html: Atomic separations of 0.14 nm and 0.26 nm have gaps of 6.0 eV and 1.0 eV. Unknown: 𝐸<sub>𝑔</sub> at 𝑑= 0.18 nm.
The gap shrinks as atoms are spaced farther apart. Between two known points on a smoothly falling curve, linear interpolation gives a good estimate.
The separation 0.18 nm is <sup>0.18</sup><sup> −</sup><sup>0.14</sup> <sub>0.26</sub><sub> −</sub><sub>0.14</sub> of the way from the first point to the second.

answer.html: 𝐸<sub>𝑔</sub>≈4.3 eV (an estimate between 6.0 eV and 1.0 eV)

check.html: The value lies between the two known gaps, and 4.3 eV is close to the insulator range.

items.title: Get It? (p. 652): A student says that electrons in the conduction band of a silicon chip are held tightly in chemical bonds between neighboring atoms. Is that correct? Explain how the valence band and conduction band differ

body.html: The statement is not correct. Electrons held in bonds belong to the valence band, which is the lower-energy band. Electrons in the conduction band have more energy and are free to move through the crystal, so they carry current.

answer.html: No. Bonded electrons are in the lower-energy valence band; conduction-band electrons are free, higher-energy, current-carrying electrons.

check.html: An electron must gain at least the gap energy to move from the valence band to the conduction band, which fits "free" electrons having more energy.

items.title: Figure 2 prompt: A wire coating must keep current from leaking out of a copper wire. Explain why a large forbidden gap is desirable for this coating, and why a conductor wants the opposite

body.html: Electrons need at least the gap energy to reach the conduction band. A large gap means almost no electrons can get there, so almost no free charge carriers exist and the coating does not conduct. A conductor needs many free carriers, so it wants a very small gap (or none).

answer.html: A large gap leaves essentially no free carriers, so the coating insulates; a conductor needs a small gap so that many electrons are in the conduction band.

check.html: Consistent with the trend that conductivity falls as the gap increases.

items.title: Get It? (p. 652): A smartphone processor is cut from a silicon wafer. How would you describe the conductivity of silicon?

body.html: Silicon is a semiconductor. Its conductivity is much lower than that of a metal and much higher than that of an insulator, and it can be changed by doping, temperature, and light. (The phone's copper traces are conductors and its plastic case is an insulator.)

answer.html: Silicon's conductivity is intermediate and controllable: between a conductor's and an insulator's.

check.html: This controllability is what lets one crystal serve as wires, resistors, diodes, and transistors.

items.title: Get It? (p. 653): Porcelain insulators hold a power line on a utility pole. Explain why an insulator such as porcelain does not conduct electric charge

body.html: In an insulator the valence band is full, the conduction band is empty, and the forbidden gap is at least about 5 eV. Thermal energy at ordinary temperatures is only a few hundredths of an eV, so essentially no electrons are lifted into the conduction band, and no free charges carry current.

answer.html: The forbidden gap is too large for electrons to cross, so there are essentially no free charge carriers.

check.html: Insulators are used because they keep current out of the pole and away from people.

items.title: 1 (Lesson 1, Example 1 Practice 1): Magnesium has 2 free electrons per atom, a density of 1.74 g/cm³, and an atomic mass of 24.305 g/mol. How many free electrons are there per cm³?

body.html: 𝜌= 1.74 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, 𝑀= 24.305 g/mol, 2 e⁻ per atom. Find free e⁻/cm³.

answer.html: 8.62 × 10<sup>22</sup> free electrons per cm³

check.html: Same order as other metals (10<sup>22</sup> to 10<sup>23</sup> per cm³).

items.title: 2 (Example 1 Practice 2): Sodium has 1 free electron per atom, a density of 0.971 g/cm³, and an atomic mass of 22.990 g/mol. How many free electrons are there per cm³?

body.html: 𝜌= 0.971 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, 𝑀= 22.990 g/mol, 1 e⁻ per atom.

answer.html: 2.54 × 10<sup>22</sup> free electrons per cm³

check.html: Sodium is a light, low-density metal with one electron per atom, so a smaller count than magnesium's is expected.

items.title: 3 (Example 1 Practice 3): Lithium has 1 free electron per atom, a density of 0.534 g/cm³, and an atomic mass of 6.94 g/mol. How many free electrons are there per cm³?

body.html: 𝜌= 0.534 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, 𝑀= 6.94 g/mol, 1 e⁻ per atom.

answer.html: 4.63 × 10<sup>22</sup> free electrons per cm³

check.html: Lithium has a very low density but very light atoms, so its electron density is similar to other metals.

items.title: 4 (Example 1 Practice 4): Gallium has 3 free electrons per atom, a density of 5.91 g/cm³, and an atomic mass of 69.72 g/mol. How many free electrons are there per cm³?

body.html: 𝜌= 5.91 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, 𝑀= 69.72 g/mol, 3 e⁻ per atom.

answer.html: 1.53 × 10<sup>23</sup> free electrons per cm³

check.html: Three electrons per atom gives a larger count than the one- and two-electron metals above.

items.title: 5 (Example 1 Practice 5, Challenge): A bar of magnesium has a mass of 845 g. How many free electrons does it contain?

body.html: Mass 𝑚= 845 g, 𝑛= 8.62 × 10<sup>22</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> (problem 1), 𝜌= 1.74 g/cm<sup>3</sup>. Find the total number of free electrons.
Find the volume from mass and density, then multiply by the electron density.

answer.html: about 4.19 × 10<sup>25</sup> free electrons

check.html: About 486 cm³ times a number near 10<sup>22</sup> to 10<sup>23</sup> gives about 10<sup>25</sup>; reasonable.

items.title: Get It? (p. 655): A toaster's heating element is a metal wire, and a thermostat contains a semiconductor sensor. As both heat up, how does the change in conductivity of the wire compare with that of the sensor?

body.html: In a metal, higher temperature makes the electrons collide more often with the atoms, so conductivity falls. In a semiconductor, higher temperature gives more electrons enough energy to cross the gap, so conductivity rises.

answer.html: The wire's conductivity decreases as it heats up; the semiconductor sensor's conductivity increases.

check.html: This opposite trend is why a semiconductor makes a good temperature sensor.

items.title: 1 (Lesson 1, Example 2 Practice 1): A germanium crystal at 290 K has 1.38 × 1013 free electrons per cm³. Germanium has 𝜌= 5.32 g/cm3 and 𝑀= 72.6 g/mol. How many free electrons are there per atom?

body.html: 𝑛= 1.38 × 10<sup>13</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>, 𝜌= 5.32 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, 𝑀= 72.6 g/mol.

answer.html: 3.13 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>10</sup> free electrons per Ge atom

check.html: Far less than one per atom, as expected for a semiconductor with no doping.

items.title: 2 (Example 2 Practice 2): The same kind of germanium crystal at 220 K has 1.36 × 1011 free electrons per cm³. How many free electrons are there per atom?

body.html: 𝑛= 1.36 × 10<sup>11</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>; same 𝜌 and 𝑀 as germanium above.

answer.html: 3.08 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>12</sup> free electrons per atom

check.html: Smaller than the 290 K value in problem 1, as expected at lower temperature.

items.title: 3 (Example 2 Practice 3): The same germanium at 120.0 K has 2.75 × 104 free electrons per cm³. How many free electrons are there per atom?

body.html: 𝑛= 2.75 × 10<sup>4</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>.

answer.html: 6.23 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>19</sup> free electrons per atom

check.html: Smaller again at the lower temperature; essentially no free electrons.

items.title: 4 (Example 2 Practice 4): A germanium sample at an unknown temperature has 7.9 × 1011 free electrons per cm³. How many free electrons are there per atom?

body.html: 𝑛= 7.9 × 10<sup>11</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>.

answer.html: 1.8 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>11</sup> free electrons per atom

check.html: Between the 220 K and 290 K values, so the sample's temperature lies between those two.

items.title: 5 (Example 2 Practice 5): A silicon crystal at 150.0 K has 2.00 free electrons per cm³. Silicon has 𝜌= 2.33 g/cm3 and 𝑀= 28.09 g/mol. How many free electrons are there per atom, and what is 150.0 K in degrees Celsius?

body.html: 𝑛= 2.00 cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>, 𝜌= 2.33 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, 𝑀= 28.09 g/mol. Convert the temperature.

answer.html: 4.01 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>23</sup> free electrons per atom; 150.0 K is −123.2°C

check.html: Essentially no free electrons at such a low temperature; −123°C is far below freezing.

items.title: 6 (Example 2 Practice 6): The same silicon at 250.0 K has 1.60 × 108 free electrons per cm³. How many free electrons are there per atom, and what is 250.0 K in degrees Celsius?

body.html: 𝑛= 1.60 × 10<sup>8</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>.

answer.html: 3.20 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>15</sup> free electrons per atom; 250.0 K is −23.2°C

check.html: Larger than at 150 K and much smaller than the value at room temperature, as expected for a cold crystal.

items.title: 7 (Example 2 Practice 7, Challenge): In a silicon crystal the number of free electrons doubles for every 10.0°C (10.0 K) rise in temperature. Using the 250.0 K value from problem 6, find the free electron density at 310.0 K

body.html: 𝑛 doubles for each 10.0 K. From problem 6, 𝑛(250.0 K) = 1.60 × 10<sup>8</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>. Find 𝑛(310.0 K).
Repeated doubling means multiplying by 2<sup>𝑘</sup>, where 𝑘 is the number of 10.0 K steps.

answer.html: 1.02 × 10<sup>10</sup> free electrons per cm³

check.html: It rose by a factor of 64 over 60 K, a large but reasonable rise for a semiconductor.

items.title: Figure 7 prompt (Infer): Boron has three valence electrons. If boron atoms are added to silicon, is the crystal n-type or p-type?

body.html: Silicon has four valence electrons. A dopant with three valence electrons is one electron short of completing the bonds, so it creates a hole (an acceptor). Positive holes act as the charge carriers, which makes the crystal p-type.

answer.html: p-type

check.html: Gallium, also with three valence electrons, makes p-type silicon.

items.title: Example Problem 3, Practice Problems 1-4 (doping) Problem 1 (Lesson 1, Example 3 Practice 1): Silicon at 320 K has 6.19 × 1010 thermally freed electrons per cm³ (𝜌= 2.33 g/cm3, 𝑀= 28.09 g/mol). How many phosphorus atoms per silicon atom must be added so that the phosphorus supplies 5.0 × 103 times as many free electrons as thermal excitation does? Each phosphorus atom gives one electron.

body.html: Thermal electrons per atom: first convert 𝑛 to a per-atom value. Doped electrons wanted: 5.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> times that. One electron per P atom.

answer.html: 6.2 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>9</sup> phosphorus atoms per silicon atom (about 6 per billion)

check.html: A tiny fraction, as expected for a required ratio of only a few thousand.

items.title: 2 (Example 3 Practice 2): Germanium at 320 K has 5.50 × 1013 thermal electrons per cm³ (

question.html: 𝜌= 5.32 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, 𝑀= 72.6 g/mol). How many phosphorus atoms per germanium atom give 2.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> times the thermal electrons?

body.html: 𝑛= 5.50 × 10<sup>13</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>; ratio wanted 2.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>.

answer.html: 2.5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> phosphorus atoms per germanium atom

check.html: Larger than in problem 1 because germanium has many more thermal carriers to overcome.

items.title: 3 (Example 3 Practice 3): Silicon at 450.0 K has 3.64 × 1013 thermal electrons per cm³. It is doped with one phosphorus atom per 2.0 × 106 silicon atoms. Find the ratio of doped electrons to thermal electrons. Use 𝜌= 2.33 g/cm3 and 𝑀= 28.09 g/mol.

body.html: Thermal carriers 3.64 × 10<sup>13</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>. Find silicon atoms per cm³, then the doped carrier density.

answer.html: about 6.9 × 10<sup>2</sup> doped electrons per thermal electron

check.html: Doping still dominates at 450 K, but the ratio is much smaller than at room temperature, since many more electrons are freed thermally.

items.title: (Ge: 4.41 × 1022 atoms/cm³; Si: 4.99 × 1022 atoms/cm³). Which material is better, and why? (Estimate.)

body.html: A device works as designed only while the doped carriers outnumber the thermal ones.

The temperature rise is 130 −25 = 105°C. 𝑛<sub>Ge</sub> = (2.0 × 10<sup>13</sup>) 2<sup>105 / 13</sup> = (2.0 × 10<sup>13</sup>)(270) = 5.4 × 10<sup>15</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> 𝑛<sub>Si</sub> = (1.5 × 10<sup>10</sup>) 2<sup>105 / 8</sup> = (1.5 × 10<sup>10</sup>)(8.9 × 10<sup>3</sup>) = 1.3 × 10<sup>14</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> Doped carriers are about 4.4 × 10<sup>16</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> (Ge) and 5.0 × 10<sup>16</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> (Si). The ratios of doped to thermal carriers are:

answer.html: Silicon is better. At 130°C the doped carriers outnumber thermal ones by only about 8 to 1 in germanium but by about 370 to 1 in silicon (rough estimate).

check.html: Germanium's smaller gap gives it far more thermal carriers, so its controlled behavior is lost at a lower temperature, matching the trend in the lesson.

items.title: Get It? (p. 659): A coffee maker uses a thermistor to sense the water temperature. As the water gets hotter, what happens to the thermistor's conductivity and resistance?

body.html: A thermistor is a semiconductor device. As temperature rises, more electrons enter the conduction band, so its conductivity rises and its resistance falls.

answer.html: Conductivity increases and resistance decreases as the water heats up.

check.html: This is opposite to a metal wire, as expected.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) Problem 1: Gallium arsenide has a forbidden gap of 1.4 eV. Is it a conductor, a semiconductor, or an insulator?

body.html: A gap of about 1 eV is the semiconductor range (insulators are 5 eV or more).

answer.html: Semiconductor

check.html: 1.4 eV is close to silicon's 1.1 eV and far below the 5 to 10 eV insulator range.

items.title: 2: In which type of material are electrons most free to move between atoms?

body.html: In a conductor, the bands overlap or the conduction band is partly filled, so electrons move freely. In a semiconductor they move only after crossing a small gap, and in an insulator they stay with their atoms.

answer.html: In a conductor

check.html: Opposite of an insulator, where electrons stay with the same atom.

items.title: 3: Sapphire (aluminum oxide) has a forbidden gap of about 9 eV. Is it more useful as a conductor or as an insulator?

body.html: A 9 eV gap is in the insulator range, so it does not conduct. That makes it useful for insulating layers.

answer.html: It is more useful as an insulator.

check.html: A gap of 9 eV is much larger than thermal energies, so almost no carriers are available.

items.title: 4: A chip designer needs a region of silicon that can carry a signal current between two components. Should the region be doped n-type or left intrinsic (undoped)?

body.html: Doping adds donor electrons or holes, which increases conductivity. Undoped silicon has very few carriers (about 10<sup>10</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> at room temperature), so it conducts poorly.

answer.html: Dope it (n-type), because doping adds charge carriers and increases the conductivity.

check.html: Doping raises the carrier count by many orders of magnitude, as in Example Problem 3.

items.title: 5 (Critical Thinking): A student argues that germanium is the better choice for a sensor that must work up to 200°C because its smaller gap makes it conduct better. Evaluate this argument

body.html: For a device, what matters is the size of the thermal carrier number compared with the doped carrier number, not the total conductivity.

Germanium does conduct better, but only because it has many more thermally freed electrons, and those are uncontrolled. As the temperature rises, thermal carriers in germanium grow to the level of the doped carriers at a much lower temperature than in silicon, so the doping no longer controls the device.

answer.html: The argument is wrong. Germanium's small gap gives so many thermal carriers that they overwhelm the doped carriers at a lower temperature, so silicon is the better material for high temperatures.

check.html: At 130°C, silicon still has doped carriers outnumbering thermal ones by hundreds to one, while germanium does not.

question.html: Work (model response): Examples from this lesson: Structure and Function (the crystal structure and dopants determine how well a material conducts); Cause and Effect (raising the temperature of a semiconductor frees more electrons, so conductivity increases); Energy and Matter (an electron needs at least the gap energy to enter the conduction band); Patterns (conductivity trends with gap size); Scale and Proportion (a few dopant atoms per billion change conductivity by factors of thousands).

answer.html: Open-ended; sample table entries are given above.

check.html: Each entry points to a specific statement in the lesson.

items.title: Review the News (a news story about solar cells or LEDs)

body.html: This asks the student to find and evaluate a current news story about a semiconductor device such as a solar cell or an LED lighting product, so no single answer exists. A good response names the source, checks that it is reliable (author, date, evidence), and summarizes the main finding in plain language, including which semiconductor property (gap, doping, or junction) the story relies on.

answer.html: Individual research task; no unique answer. See the method above.

check.html: The summary should be traceable to a named source.

items.title: Focus Question: What is the difference between conductors, insulators, and semiconductors?

body.html: Band theory. Conductivity depends on the energy gap between the valence band and the conduction band.

In a conductor the bands overlap or the conduction band is partly filled, so electrons move freely. In an insulator the valence band is full and the forbidden gap is large (about 5 to 10 eV), so almost no electrons reach the conduction band. In a semiconductor the gap is small (about 1 eV), so some electrons are thermally excited across it.

answer.html: Conductors have no gap (overlapping or partly filled bands), semiconductors have a small gap (about 1 eV), and insulators have a large gap (5 eV or more).

check.html: The ordering of gap size matches the ordering of conductivity in Figure 2.

items.title: Figure 1 prompt: Estimate the energy gap of a material with an atomic separation of 0.2 nm

body.html: Atomic separation 𝑑= 0.2 nm. Unknown: gap 𝐸<sub>𝑔</sub>. From Figure 1: carbon (at about 0.15 nm) has a 5.5 eV gap; silicon (at about 0.24 nm) has a 1.1 eV gap.

On the graph, the gap is the vertical distance between the lowest edge of the conduction band and the highest edge of the valence band at the chosen separation. The gap shrinks as atoms are spaced farther apart (up to the point where the bands cross).

Reading the graph at 0.2 nm, the lowest edge of the conduction band and the top edge of the valence band are between the carbon and silicon lines. Using the carbon and silicon gaps for scale, the separation 0.2 nm lies between 0.15 nm and 0.24 nm, so the gap lies between 5.5 eV and 1.1 eV. Linear interpolation gives:

answer.html: 𝐸<sub>𝑔</sub>≈3 eV (an estimate read from the graph; between carbon's 5.5 eV and silicon's 1.1 eV)

check.html: The value lies between the two labeled gaps, as it should, and 3 eV is a poor-conductor (wide-gap semiconductor) gap.

items.title: Get It? (p. 652): What is the difference between the valence band and the conduction band?

body.html: The valence band is the lower-energy band; its electrons are bound in the crystal's bonds. The conduction band is the higher-energy band; electrons there are free to move through the crystal and carry current.

answer.html: The valence band holds bonded electrons (lower energy); the conduction band holds free, current-carrying electrons (higher energy).

check.html: This matches the text: lower regions are bonding, higher regions allow motion between atoms.

items.title: Figure 2 prompt: Explain why a small forbidden gap is more desirable than a large forbidden gap for a conductor

body.html: Electrons must gain at least the gap energy to move into the conduction band, where they can carry current. A small gap means a small energy input (such as thermal energy or the work done by a small electric field) frees many electrons, so the material conducts well. A large gap means very few electrons can ever reach the conduction band.

answer.html: A small gap requires little energy to put electrons into the conduction band, so more charge carriers are available and conductivity is higher.

check.html: Consistent with Figure 2 (conductivity increases as the gap decreases).

items.title: Get It? (p. 652): How would you describe the conductivity of the material at the beginning of this module?

body.html: The opening photo shows a circuit board and a silicon chip. The chip's material is silicon, a semiconductor, so its conductivity is intermediate: far lower than a metal's and far higher than an insulator's, and it can be controlled by doping, temperature, and light. (The board's copper traces are conductors; the plastic board is an insulator.)

answer.html: The chip material (silicon) is a semiconductor: moderate, controllable conductivity between that of conductors and insulators.

check.html: Fits the module's theme of controlling conductivity in electronic components.

items.title: Get It? (p. 653): Explain why insulators do not conduct electric charges

body.html: In an insulator the valence band is full and the conduction band is empty, with a gap of at least 5 eV. Electrons' thermal energy at room temperature is only a few hundredths of an eV, and a small electric field adds little, so almost no electrons are lifted into the conduction band.

answer.html: The forbidden gap (at least 5 eV) is too large for electrons to cross, so essentially no free charge carriers exist.

check.html: Matches the book's statement that insulators coat wires to prevent shorting.

answer.html: about 1.90 × 10<sup>26</sup> free electrons

items.title: Get It? (p. 655): How is the effect of temperature on conductivity different for metals than for semiconductors?

body.html: In a metal, higher temperature makes the electrons move faster and collide more often with atomic cores, which lowers conductivity. In a semiconductor, higher temperature gives more electrons enough energy to cross the gap, which raises conductivity.

answer.html: Metals conduct worse as temperature rises; semiconductors conduct better.

check.html: Same trend as the thermistor, which has falling resistance with rising temperature.

answer.html: 3.78 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>18</sup> free electrons per atom; 200.0 K is −73.2°C

check.html: Larger than at 100 K and smaller than the room-temperature value 2.90 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>13</sup>.

items.title: 7 (Example 2 Practice 7, Challenge): Silicon at 264 K

body.html: 𝑛 doubles for each 8.00°C (8.00 K) rise. From problem 6, 𝑛(200 K) = 1.89 × 10<sup>5</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>. Find 𝑛(264 K).
Repeated doubling means multiplying by 2<sup>𝑘</sup>, where 𝑘 is the number of 8-K steps.

answer.html: 4.84 × 10<sup>7</sup> free electrons per cm³

check.html: It rose by a factor of 256 over 64 K, which is a large but reasonable rise for a semiconductor.

items.title: Figure 7 prompt (Infer): Antimony has five valence electrons. n-type or p-type?

body.html: Silicon has four valence electrons. A dopant with five valence electrons (like arsenic) supplies one extra "donor" electron, which makes the crystal n-type (negative carriers).

answer.html: n-type

check.html: Same as arsenic, which also has five valence electrons.

items.title: Example Problem 3, Practice Problems 1-4 (doping) Problem 1 (Lesson 1, Example 3 Practice 1): Arsenic atoms per silicon atom for 104 times the thermal electrons

body.html: Thermal free electrons in silicon at room temperature: 2.90 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>13</sup> per atom (Example Problem 2). Arsenic electrons wanted: 1 × 10<sup>4</sup> times that. One electron per As atom.

answer.html: 2.9 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>9</sup> arsenic atoms per silicon atom (about 3 per billion)

check.html: A tiny fraction, much less than the one-in-a-million of Example Problem 3, as expected for a smaller required ratio.

items.title: 2 (Example 3 Practice 2): Germanium, 5000 times the thermal electrons

body.html: Ge thermal electrons: 5.19 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>9</sup> per atom. Ratio wanted: 5 × 10<sup>3</sup>.

answer.html: 2.6 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>5</sup> arsenic atoms per germanium atom

check.html: Larger than the silicon answer because germanium has far more thermal carriers to overcome.

items.title: 3 (Example 3 Practice 3): Silicon at 400.0 K, 1 As per million Si

body.html: Thermal carriers 4.54 × 10<sup>12</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>. Doped carriers from Example 3: 4.99 × 10<sup>16</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>.

answer.html: about 1.10 × 10<sup>4</sup> doped carriers per thermal carrier

check.html: Smaller than the room-temperature ratio of 3.44 × 10<sup>6</sup>, since more carriers are thermally freed at 400 K, but doping still dominates.

items.title: 4 (Example 3 Practice 4, Challenge): Germanium versus silicon devices above the boiling point of water

body.html: Germanium's gap (0.7 eV) is smaller than silicon's (1.1 eV), so germanium has many more thermal carriers at any temperature. If thermal carriers become comparable to the doped carriers, the device loses its controlled behavior.

At 400 K (above 373 K, the boiling point of water), silicon still has doped carriers 10<sup>4</sup> times thermal ones. For germanium, at room temperature thermal carriers are already 2.25 × 10<sup>13</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> (about 1500 times silicon's), and with the book's doubling every 13°C the Ge value at about 400 K rises to roughly 5 × 10<sup>15</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>. One As per million Ge atoms gives only about 4 × 10<sup>16</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup>, a ratio of only about 10 (a rough estimate).

answer.html: Above about 100 °C, thermally freed carriers swamp the doped carriers in germanium, so germanium devices fail to behave as designed, while silicon devices keep working. Silicon is better for high temperatures.

check.html: This agrees with the book's statement that germanium is too temperature-sensitive for many applications.

items.title: Get It? (p. 659): Describe the relationship between temperature and conductivity in a thermistor

body.html: A thermistor is a semiconductor device; as temperature rises, more electrons enter the conduction band, so its conductivity rises and its resistance falls.

answer.html: Conductivity increases (resistance decreases) as temperature increases.

check.html: Opposite to a metal wire, as the text says.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) Problem 1: Magnesium oxide, forbidden gap of 8 eV

body.html: A gap of 5 to 10 eV is the insulator range.

answer.html: Insulator

check.html: 8 eV is much larger than the semiconductor gap of about 1 eV.

items.title: 2: Where are electrons most likely to remain with the same atom?

body.html: In an insulator, electrons are tightly held in the full valence band and cannot reach the conduction band. In conductors and (to a lesser degree) semiconductors, electrons move between atoms.

answer.html: In an insulator

check.html: Opposite of a conductor, where electrons move freely.

items.title: 3: Silicon dioxide with a 9 eV gap

body.html: A 9 eV gap is in the insulator range, so it does not conduct. That makes it useful for insulating layers in chips.

answer.html: It is more useful as an insulator.

check.html: The book says silicon dioxide insulation is grown on chips by exposure to oxygen.

items.title: 4: Region of an integrated circuit with good insulating properties

body.html: Doping adds donor electrons or holes, which increases conductivity. Leaving the silicon undoped (intrinsic) leaves very few carriers (about 1.45 × 10<sup>10</sup> cm<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> at room temperature), so it conducts poorly.

answer.html: Leave the region as intrinsic (undoped) silicon, because doping would add charge carriers and reduce its insulating ability.

check.html: Consistent with Example Problem 3, where doping raised carriers by a factor of a million.

items.title: 5 (Critical Thinking): Why germanium is not better at high temperature

body.html: The doubling rate describes how quickly the number of carriers grows, but what matters for a device is how large the thermal carrier number is compared with the doped carrier number.

Germanium's carrier number doubles more slowly per degree (13°C versus 8°C), but germanium starts with far more thermal carriers (its smaller gap gives about 1500 times as many as silicon at room temperature). Thermal carriers in germanium reach the level of the doped carriers at a much lower temperature than in silicon, so the device's behavior is lost earlier.

answer.html: Germanium has so many thermal carriers to begin with (smaller gap) that they overwhelm the doped carriers at a lower temperature than in silicon, so silicon is the better high-temperature material.

check.html: At 400 K silicon's doped carriers still outnumber thermal ones about 10<sup>4</sup> to 1 (Lesson 1, Example 3 Practice 3).
